findings.detail: The paper reports that the council's Housing Central Rents Team has increased direct Universal Credit payments and pursued outstanding tenant debt where Universal Credit is not in place. It also notes the Rent Assistance Fund, introduced in 2023, for tenants facing hardship.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing housing revenue collection with peer councils can see the council reporting collection above both the Scottish and Local Authority averages.
findings.figures: Rent collection 100.03% (2025/26); Scottish average 99.7%; Scottish LA average 99.6%
findings.quote: Our rent collection levels for 2025 /26 were 100.03% (rounded to 100% on the SHR website) which is slightly higher than the Scottish average of 99.7% and the Scottish LA average of 99.6%.

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Office Accommodation shows a £1.584m outturn underspend in the expenditure table, with no explanation given in the narrative.
findings.detail: The table shows a revised budget of £4,344,155 for Office Accommodation, actual spend of £120,339 and committed spend of £2,260,173, giving an outturn of £2,760,173. The narrative section does not discuss this variance.
findings.matters: A large underspend that the report does not explain is one a finance director would want to ask about, as it affects the trend-based adjustment and borrowing assumptions.
findings.figures: £4,344,155 revised budget; £120,339 actual; £2,260,173 committed; £2,760,173 outturn; £1,583,982 outturn variance
findings.quote: CXA1C Office Accommodation 4,344,155.00

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: The report says all service areas continue to face 'significant challenges' delivering capital programmes within available resources, citing continuing increases in the cost of delivery.
findings.detail: The report states that the service will continue to seek to manage within existing resources. The Measures of Success section says the service aims to be in a balanced budget position at year-end and will take current reprofile requests to Committee.
findings.matters: The service links cost increases in capital delivery to its ability to stay within its envelope, which is the same funding pressure finance directors across councils are managing.
findings.figures: Not stated in paper
findings.quote: all service areas continue to face significant challenges managing the delivery of capital programmes within the available envelope of resources.

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Assets and Procurement forecasts £3.188m under budget, with the report attributing the Maintaining Existing Assets variance to toilet, rewiring, re-roofing and window projects that are at design stage or delayed.
findings.detail: The Maintaining Existing Assets theme is forecast £1.346m below budget. The report says the toilet upgrades, Netherton Primary rewire (now starting April 2027), the Shotts Community Centre and St Aidan's re-roofing, and the Holy Cross window replacement (now 2027/28) are not expected to progress this year. Targeted Investment slippage of £1.116m is also reported.
findings.matters: Slippage across condition-based maintenance is a recurring pattern for councils managing a large estate, and the report's explanations show it coming from design and procurement timing rather than funding.
findings.figures: £3.188m Assets and Procurement underspend; £1.346m Maintaining Existing Assets; £1.116m Targeted Investment slippage; £0.580m Netherton Primary
findings.quote: forecast expenditure is £1.346m below budget this financial year.

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Clyde Valley High School scope is under review, with the report saying the solution has a significantly higher financial impact and the project will go to a future capital bid.
findings.detail: The Sustainable Estate theme shows a £0.252m variance. The Clyde Valley High School works are £0.138m of this, and the Holytown Primary School works (£0.120m) have been put on hold while their scope is reviewed.
findings.matters: A school project moving out of the current programme and into a new capital bid because of cost is a re-prioritisation that other councils' finance officers would track against their own capital plans.
findings.figures: £0.252m Sustainable Estate variance; £0.138m Clyde Valley High School; £0.120m Holytown Primary School
findings.quote: This project will now be subject to a future capital bid.

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: The Demolitions theme is projecting £0.540m above budget, mainly because the Ravenswood Primary project is forecast £1.342m over due to enhanced specifications.
findings.detail: The report says the Ravenswood Primary overspend follows enhanced specifications being added to the project. This is partly offset by the Motherwell Concert Hall project, where progress depends on ongoing considerations, and by the 124 Main Street project, which is on hold until 2027/28.
findings.matters: A specification change added during delivery, rather than a delivery delay, is the cause of the overspend, which is the sort of scope-driven cost growth finance directors monitor on school capital programmes.
findings.figures: £0.540m theme overspend; £1.342m Ravenswood Primary overspend; £0.639m Motherwell Concert Hall; £0.200m 124 Main Street
findings.quote: This overspend is due to enhanced specifications being incorporated into the project, resulting in higher costs than originally budgeted.

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Pather Cemetery is forecast £0.720m over budget, with the report saying cost rose during construction because of civil engineering design challenges and architectural re-designs.
findings.detail: The cemetery was completed in July 2026. The report lists increased burial capacity, on-site car parking, internal roads, a visitor building and a SUDs system as delivered, and says costs rose during construction because of civil engineering design challenges and architectural re-designs to resolve emerging roofing issues.
findings.matters: A completed scheme reporting an overspend driven by design problems found during construction shows the cost-control risk that finance officers at other councils are managing on their own capital builds.
findings.figures: £0.720m overspend (Pather Cemetery); Greenspace and Cemeteries theme £0.796m over budget
findings.quote: Cost rose during construction due to civil engineering design challenges experienced in construction

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: The Parks Masterplan theme projects a £6.968m underspend on the Watersports Centre, while updated forecasts show the overall project expected to exceed its current estimate.
findings.detail: The Water Source Heat Pump is still in design and affecting planning consent for the plant room, and financial close has been re-programmed to late Q1/early Q2 2027. The report says the project continues to experience cost pressures, and the rising costs are being assessed through the Strategic Capital Delivery Group Emerging Priorities Protocol.
findings.matters: A large underspend from delayed start dates alongside a forecast cost increase on the same scheme is a pattern other councils' finance officers would recognise, and the report says the further increase will require consideration as the project progresses.

findings.paper_title: Enterprise and Communities - Capital Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Enterprise and Communities projects a break-even 2026/27 capital position at Period 6, with an £11.485m service underspend offset against the trend-based adjustment.

findings.matters: A break-even projection that depends on netting an underspend against a 10% trend-based adjustment shows how the outturn is being reconciled to the approved budget, and the adjustment is also used to inform the Treasury Management Strategy and borrowing needs.

findings.paper_title: Contract Award for Purchase of 70 x Hybrid Cars
findings.headline: Toyota GB PLC contract for 70 hybrid cars awarded at a maximum £979.757.10 exclusive of VAT, with a unit cost below the pre-tender estimate
findings.detail: The paper says the contract achieved a unit cost of £13,656.53 per vehicle including delivery, against a pre-tender estimate of £14,027 per vehicle. findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: The council reported a £7 million underspend against budget in 2025/26 and has a strong track record of delivering savings, though future delivery will become increasingly difficult.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget of £1,087.5 million was underspent by £7 million, with the favourable variance primarily from financing costs. The council achieved £5.9 million of £6.6 million planned savings in 2025/26, meeting the £0.7 million shortfall through alternative savings. The audit notes a 'strong track record of delivering savings' but observes that 'the scope for further savings is narrowing' and 'achieving future savings will require more difficult decisions'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to distinguish between operational budget management (which is clearly sound) and structural savings capability. The audit's observation that scope is narrowing is material: it suggests the council is approaching limits of efficiency gains and will need service-level transformation, not just efficiencies.
findings.figures: 2025/26 underspend £7 million; savings delivered £5.9 million of £6.6 million planned
findings.quote: While the council continues to deliver savings and has arrangements in place to address shortfalls, increasing financial pressures mean that achieving future savings targets is likely to require more difficult decisions

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: CIPFA's infrastructure asset valuation methodology has been discontinued, leaving the council without a permanent accounting solution for a material asset class.
findings.detail: The revised HM Treasury approach to public-sector asset valuations required local authorities to revalue infrastructure assets using CIPFA indexation in 2024/25 and 2025/26, with the approach ending for the 2024/25 financial statements. CIPFA states 'this will continue to be an area of enhanced scrutiny for local government auditors' and no permanent solution has yet been agreed.
findings.matters: Infrastructure assets are material on council balance sheets. Without agreed valuation methodology, there is ongoing uncertainty about reported asset values and the basis on which financial statements can be audited consistently.
findings.figures: Infrastructure asset valuation approach ended for 2024/25; solution is outstanding
findings.quote: a permanent solution has not yet been agreed and CIPFA believe that this will continue to be an area of enhanced scrutiny for local government auditors

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased £85.3m to £774.9m supporting capital expenditure of £304.9m, within prudential limits and Treasury Management Strategy
findings.detail: The council increased long-term borrowing from £689.6 million to £774.9 million, and capital expenditure increased to £304.9 million (up £88.2 million from prior year). Total capital investment is planned at £1.7 billion over five years, supported by the Community Investment Fund. The audit notes that 'total external debt... was within the authorised limit and operational boundary set in the Treasury Management Strategy' and 'complies with the Prudential Code'.
findings.matters: A material increase in borrowing to fund capital investment signals either confidence in long-term revenue generation or optimism about the council's ability to service the debt despite the declared budget gap. The scale (£1.7bn planned) is material relative to the council's size.
findings.figures: Borrowing increased from £689.6 million to £774.9 million; capital expenditure £304.9 million in year; £1.7 billion planned over five years
findings.quote: the council increased its long-term borrowing from £689.6 million at 31 March 2025 to £774.9 million at 31 March 2026... Total capital expenditure in 2025/26 was £304.9 million which is an increase of £88.2 million since last year

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: The council reported a related-party disclosure initially failed to include transactions worth £67.4 million in income with other Scottish public sector bodies, corrected only during the audit.
findings.detail: The draft annual accounts initially omitted disclosure of transactions with other Scottish public bodies (which are related parties under common government control). The audit required the council to review and correct this, adding disclosures of £67.4 million income, £8.3 million expenditure, and a further £1.8 million for organisations where council members are represented.
findings.matters: Completeness of related-party disclosure is a fundamental governance and transparency issue. The failure to identify £67.4 million of material transactions without audit prompting indicates a process gap in financial governance.
findings.figures: £67.4 million income; £8.3 million expenditure; £1.8 million additional
findings.quote: the council's related party disclosure note did not include transactions with other Scottish public sector bodies... Following this review, the council updated the related party disclosure note to disclose income transactions of £67.4 million, and expenditure transactions of £8.3 million in relation to transactions with Scottish public sector bodies

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: The council lacks assured control over externally hosted IT systems and has not yet implemented the auditor's prior recommendation on this issue.
findings.detail: Three critical systems (PECOS purchase-to-pay, Pay360 cash receipting, and iTrent payroll) are hosted by external cloud providers. The council does not have required assurance over its IT operations, and the auditor's prior-year recommendation to establish this has not been implemented. This remains a brought-forward audit risk for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Financial systems hosted externally without proper council assurance over access controls and data security create operational and reputational risk. The failure to implement this recommendation over time suggests either lack of capacity or prioritization.
findings.figures: Three systems in scope: PECOS (Elcom), Pay360 (The Access Group), iTrent (MHR)
findings.quote: There remains a risk for 2025/26 that the council does not have the required assurance over its IT operations

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: Internal controls over council tax and non-domestic rates discounts were not operating for most of 2025/26 following a system upgrade.
findings.detail: A secondary review control over council tax and non-domestic rates discounts, reliefs and exemptions was suspended from August 2025 following system issues from a CIVICA upgrade. The control did not operate for a significant part of the financial year, increasing the risk that discounts could be applied without appropriate review. The control resumed in July 2026. Additional audit testing found no material impact, but this represents a control failure.
findings.matters: A council's ability to control discounts and reliefs directly affects revenue collection and the financial sustainability of its budget. Suspension of key controls for nine months without compensating procedures creates compliance and revenue risk.
findings.figures: Control suspended August 2025 to July 2026
findings.quote: the council's secondary review control over council tax and non-domestic rates discounts, reliefs and exemptions was suspended from August 2025 following system issues arising from a CIVICA system upgrade. As a result, the control was not operating for a significant part of the financial year

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: The council's usable reserves have increased by £22 million to £368.3 million, creating tension with the declared structural budget deficit.
findings.detail: General Fund reserves increased to £299.8 million, with the contingency fund now at £11.8 million (matching the 1% target per the revised reserves policy) and future budget pressures reserve at £19.4 million. However, the council faces a stated budget gap of £75.5 million over three years. The Accounts Commission has specifically flagged concern that 'the council should reassess the purpose and scale of its reserves held in order to address the budget gap'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether reserves are genuinely a prudent buffer or whether they represent the council's inability or unwillingness to take difficult budget decisions. The Accounts Commission's concern suggests the former interpretation.
findings.figures: Reserves increased from £346.3 million to £368.3 million; contingency fund £11.8 million; future budget pressures reserve £19.4 million
findings.quote: The level of usable reserves held by the council increased from £346.3 million in 2024/25 to £368.3 million in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: Common good assets of up to £12.5 million remain on the council's balance sheet without clear title, representing an uncorrected misstatement.
findings.detail: The auditor identified common good assets potentially overstated by £12.5 million on the balance sheet (the council estimates £9.5 million overstatement). These assets relate to matters of rights and obligations that are complex and unresolved. The misstatement was not corrected, and the auditor and council disagree on the quantum of potential overstatement.
findings.matters: A lender reviewing the council's asset base needs to understand whether assets on the balance sheet are genuinely owned by the council or held in trust. An overstatement of equity by this magnitude affects creditworthiness assessment.
findings.figures: £12.5 million (auditor estimate); £9.5 million (council estimate) uncorrected misstatement
findings.quote: Common good assets are currently held on the council balance sheet... The auditor considers the maximum potential overstatement to be £12.5 million

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: Creditors control processes have material weaknesses, with £6.1 million of uncorrected misstatements relating to unsupported and historic balances.
findings.detail: Audit testing found £20.3 million held in a creditors suspense code, of which only £2.6 million was supported by evidence. A £13.4 million classification error was corrected. However, £4.3 million remains uncorrected (no supporting evidence) and £1.8 million of historic creditor balances dating back to 2001 should be derecognised but were not. The audit identifies 'weaknesses in the council's processes for reviewing, evidencing and classifying creditor balances'.
findings.matters: Creditors balances affect both liabilities on the balance sheet and reported expenditure; unsupported balances indicate weak financial controls even if not material to the overall statements. The age and lack of evidence for balances from 2001 suggests operational processes are not clearing old items.
findings.figures: £20.3 million in suspense code (£2.6 million supported); £13.4 million misclassification (corrected); £4.3 million uncorrected; £1.8 million historic from 2001 (uncorrected)
findings.quote: £20.3 million was held in a creditors suspense code. Of this amount, the council provided sufficient evidence to support £2.6 million... No evidence was provided to support the remaining £4.3 million... a further £1.8 million was identified within other creditors account codes in respect of historic creditor balances held dating back to 2001

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: The council's single trading operation failed to achieve its statutory break-even requirement for the third consecutive period.
findings.detail: The combined trading account covering building cleaning, waste management, and town centre activities reported a deficit of £0.5 million over the three-year rolling period to 31 March 2026, and remains in deficit of £0.2 million even after the IAS 19 accounting adjustment. The trading operations continue to face financial pressures relating to both service costs and income recovery.
findings.matters: Failure to achieve statutory break-even is a compliance issue and signals operational difficulties in services that were intended to be self-funding, requiring either service redesign or subsidy from the general fund.
findings.figures: £0.5 million deficit over three-year period; £0.2 million deficit after IAS 19 adjustment
findings.quote: The council reported a deficit of £0.5 million over the three-year period to 31 March 2026 which remains in a deficit of £0.2 million even after accounting for the technical accounting adjustment for IAS 19 Employee Benefits. As a result, the STO has not achieved its statutory break even objective

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Scotland Report
findings.headline: The council faces a structural budget gap of £75.5 million over three years, though this has reduced from the prior year's projection.

findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk needs to understand whether the council has a credible plan to close a structural gap of this magnitude, and whether one-off budget surpluses are masking the underlying issue.
findings.figures: £75.5 million gap to 2028/29 (reduced from £85.9 million prior year); £114.5 million gap over five years to 2031/32
findings.quote: the council continues to face significant financial challenges and must identify sustainable solutions to address its projected budget gap

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027-2030

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027-2030
findings.headline: Prescribing remains most significant financial risk with 5% annual growth assumption and volatile history
findings.detail: Prescribing is identified as the partnership's most significant financial risk, driven by national pricing, market conditions and clinical activity levels. A 5% annual growth assumption generates £4.432m pressure in 2027/28 alone, despite marginal underspend in 2025/26.

findings.detail: The partnership's 2026/27 savings and transformation programme has not been fully embedded, with service redesign initiatives taking longer than planned to deliver recurring benefits. findings.committee: Health and Social Care Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: IJB Annual Performance Report 2025/26
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget approved as balanced but report identifies it rests on delivery of transformation that has proved difficult to achieve
findings.detail: The IJB approved a 'balanced budget for 2026/27' in the executive summary. However, the financial section notes that 'delivery of planned savings remained challenging' in 2025/26, that the partnership is 'operating within a challenging environment' with 'demand exceeding planned levels,' and that 'further transformation is required to ensure long-term sustainability.' The pathway to the balanced 2026/27 position is not explicitly described and appears to depend on transformation initiatives that have not yet fully landed.
findings.matters: If a balanced budget depends on transformation programmes that were only partially achieved in the prior year, there is material risk of further variances in 2026/27. This is typical of councils using future savings assumptions before those savings are proven.
findings.figures: Total budget 2025/26: £908.422m; 2026/27 budget described as 'balanced' without detail on how; underlying transformation delivery only partial
findings.quote: The IJB approved a balanced budget for 2026/27, ensuring continued investment in prevention, early intervention, and community-based care.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: IJB Annual Performance Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Performance on adult social care experience indicators trails Scottish average across seven of nine measures
findings.detail: North Lanarkshire's Health and Care Experience Survey results show the partnership underperforming the Scottish average on most key measures of service quality and user experience. Adults supported at home report less independence (67.1% vs 73.6%), less say in their care (56.1% vs 63.9%), poorer service coordination (56.7% vs 65.0%), lower satisfaction (61.9% vs 72.1%), and less safety (64.5% vs 74.7%). This suggests either higher acuity/complexity in the population or service delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Below-average performance on user experience and independence outcomes may signal either higher-need population or inadequate service capacity. Either implies costs will continue rising and financial pressures will be sustained unless service model is fundamentally changed.
findings.quote: Performance in North Lanarkshire is broadly comparable with similar authorities and the Scottish average in many areas

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: IJB Annual Performance Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Workforce vacancies constrain capacity and limit transformation; reported as 'remaining a key risk'
findings.detail: The report describes vacancy levels as 'significant across some services' and explicitly states these vacancies impact 'the pace at which we deliver change and manage our capacity to meet the demand.' This is flagged as an ongoing risk that will 'continue to shape the Partnership's financial strategy.' Recruitment and retention challenges are framed as a constraint on achieving transformation, not a solved problem.
findings.matters: Unfilled vacancies reduce delivery capacity and constrain transformation programmes designed to improve efficiency. If positions remain vacant to control spend, actual service demand cannot be met; if filled, costs rise. Neither resolves the demand problem.
findings.figures: £3.688m underspend from vacancies and reduced pay, 'partially offset by additional agency and overtime costs'; workforce pressures explicitly listed as ongoing risk
findings.quote: Vacancy levels remain significant across some services, highlighting the importance of continued focus on workforce planning, wellbeing and support.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: IJB Annual Performance Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Care at home and care home costs overran budget by £2.623m due to demand exceeding plan
findings.detail: The partnership explicitly reported that demand for care at home and independent care home provision exceeded planned activity levels, reflecting increasing complexity of need and demographic pressures. This overspend was the single largest budget variance and signals structural demand-supply imbalance in a significant cost area. The report describes this as ongoing, not one-off.
findings.matters: Persistent demand exceeding plan in a demand-driven service (social care) typically cannot be solved by efficiency alone and may signal need for either service rationing or sustained subsidy. This directly affects financial resilience.
findings.figures: £2.623m overspend on Payments to Other Bodies; total IJB budget £908.422m, of which social care is a material proportion
findings.quote: Ongoing demand pressures within Care at Home and Independent Care Homes continue to exceed planned activity levels, reflecting increased complexity and volume of care packages.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: External Auditor’s Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: 2025/26 surplus of £27.263 million driven by additional partner funding, not operational performance
findings.detail: The IJB reported a surplus of £27.263 million for 2025/26. This was principally because additional funding of £27 million was received in-year from partner bodies (North Lanarkshire Council and NHS Lanarkshire) and has been earmarked for use in future years. Savings programmes of £14.959 million were identified but only £9.107 million were achieved, with the shortfall covered by underspends and additional funding.
findings.matters: The surplus masks underlying financial stress: only 61% of planned savings were delivered in-year, and the apparent surplus depends on non-recurring additional partner funding rather than sustainable operating income.
findings.figures: Surplus £27.263 million; additional partner funding £27 million (earmarked for future); budget gap £14.959 million; savings achieved £9.107 million
findings.quote: Additional funding of £27 million was also received in year from partner bodies, which has been earmarked for use in future years for areas including unscheduled care and other health care. As a result, North Lanarkshire IJB reported a surplus on the provision of services of £27.263 million at 31 March 2026.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: External Auditor’s Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Financial sustainability rated 'Very High' risk; auditor recommends shift away from reliance on annual savings delivery
findings.detail: The auditor concludes that while the IJB has developed medium and longer-term financial plans, it continues to face challenges to financial sustainability. The auditor explicitly recommends the IJB move away from reliance on delivering significant in-year savings or cost reduction measures, as this risks short-term decision-making and is not a sustainable model.
findings.matters: This signals the lender and finance director that the current financial model is structurally unsustainable and dependent on delivering year-on-year savings programmes that may not be achievable or may compromise service delivery.
findings.figures: Risk register entries: Financial Sustainability – Medium Term rated 'Very High'; Financial Sustainability – Long Term rated 'Very High'
findings.quote: Challenges remain in delivering financial sustainability over the medium term, with significant budget gaps forecast. It is important that North Lanarkshire Integration Joint Board, working with its strategic partners, develops a financially sustainable operating model, moving away from the reliance on delivering significant in-year savings or cost reduction measures that risk short-term decision making.

findings.paper_title: Best Value Thematic Audit: Asset Management
findings.headline: Capital programme slipping in 2025/26, with only 80% of General Services capital delivered against 98% target.
findings.detail: The council approved a £310m capital programme for 2025/26, revised to £318m. Challenges cited include staffing shortages, contractor and supply chain issues, and rising costs.
findings.matters: Persistent capital programme shortfalls indicate execution risk and suggest the council may struggle to deliver its strategic asset management plans. Reprofiling creates uncertainty about project timelines and typically increases costs.

findings.quote: The latest monitoring report (as at 27 February 2026) shows slippage in programme delivery. The council has delivered: 80 per cent of the General Services capital programme (£180.276 million revised budget), compared with a target of 98 per cent of the projected outturn being committed.

findings.paper_title: Best Value Thematic Audit: Asset Management
findings.headline: Council's medium-term financial plan identifies a £75.5m funding gap for 2027/28-2029/30.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan for 2027/28-2031/32 highlights a significant funding gap of £75.545m for the three-year period from 2027/28 to 2029/30. This reflects ongoing cost pressures, high interest rates, and economic uncertainty across Scotland. The council acknowledges these risks require ongoing careful management but has not yet detailed how it will close the gap.
findings.matters: A £75.5m funding gap represents a material challenge requiring either significant service reductions or new funding sources. This indicates the council faces serious budget pressures in the medium term as rising interest costs compete with service spending.
findings.figures: £75.545m funding gap; period 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.quote: Under the envisaged scenario, it highlights a significant funding gap of £75.545 million for the three-year budget period from 2027/28 to 2029/30. It continues to monitor affordability acknowledging that risks will require ongoing careful management.

findings.paper_title: Best Value Thematic Audit: Asset Management
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased 31% to £774.9m over two years, driving up annual interest costs.
findings.detail: Long-term borrowing rose from £590.6m in 2023/24 to £774.9m in 2025/26, an increase of £184.3m. Annual interest costs increased from £44.6m to £58.2m. The Treasury Management Strategy projects financing costs will rise from 5.4% of net revenue in 2026/27 to 8.3% by 2030/31. The strategy indicates borrowing will remain sustainable but acknowledges substantial financial pressures and the need for careful ongoing management.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce resources available for service delivery and constrain financial flexibility. A 31% increase in debt over two years signals increasing reliance on borrowing to fund the capital programme.
findings.figures: £590.6m to £774.9m (31% increase); £44.6m to £58.2m interest costs; financing costs projected to rise from 5.4% to 8.3% of net revenue
findings.quote: As reported in the council's annual accounts, long-term borrowing increased from £590.6 million in 2023/24 to £774.9 million in 2025/26, a rise of 31 per cent over the period. This was accompanied by an increase in annual interest costs from £44.6 million to £58.2 million.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: PPP contract obligations increasing; prior five-year saving of £4.5 million from 2023 plan is being reversed with £1 million per annum added from year 3 onwards.
findings.detail: The June 2023 MTFP included a £4.5m saving for PPP funding over five years. The council now states: 'It was recognised that additional budgetary provision would require to be incorporated into future MTFPs. Therefore, year three to five of this plan reflects an additional cost of £1.000 million per annum. Further additional financial consequences will be recognised in future Financial Outlooks or MTFPs.' This shows prior savings assumptions were optimistic.
findings.matters: Savings being reversed mid-plan indicates planning assumptions are unreliable. Additional costs flagged as 'will be recognised in future' suggests further increases are anticipated.
findings.figures: £4.5 million prior saving (2023), £1 million per annum additional cost (year 3–5 = £3 million additional)
findings.quote: The MTFP reported in June 2023 incorporated a saving of £4.500 million for the five years... Therefore, year three to five of this plan reflects an additional cost of £1.000 million per annum.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council Tax increase limited to 7% in 2026/27 despite recommended 10%, constraining future increases; even 10% annual increase generates only £20.6m against £75.5m three-year gap.
findings.detail: In February 2026 the council chose to approve 7% (Band D £1,554.56) rather than recommended 10%. The document notes the council has the 4th lowest Band D charge nationally despite being 6th in deprivation, constraining political headroom for increases. Even at 10% annual increases, Council Tax would generate only £61.8m over three years—leaving £13.7m uncovered.
findings.matters: Council Tax is politically constrained and mathematically insufficient. The council cannot grow its way out of this gap; it must cut services or use reserves.
findings.figures: 7% increase approved (vs 10% recommended), Band D £1,554.56, 5–10% annual increase generates £10.3–20.6 million per year or £30.9–61.8 million over three years
findings.quote: However, at the budget setting meeting in February 2026/27 the Council took the decision to approve a 7 % increase to Council Tax, resulting in an increased Band D charge of £1,554.56.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Scottish Government may remove statutory capital accounting mitigations, creating uncertain but material additional revenue cost.
findings.detail: The council notes as a current 'notable risk': 'Scottish Government's plans to review the Capital Accounting arrangements and statutory mitigations in respect of such, to ensure they remain fit for purpose... Removing existing statutory mitigations will have material financial consequences on revenue budgets and ultimately potentially impacting on capital investment programmes.' No timetable or amount is specified, but the impact is flagged as 'material.'
findings.matters: This is an external policy change that could increase the effective budget gap by an unknown but material amount, or force capital programme cuts that damage service delivery.
findings.figures: Impact described as 'material' but unquantified
findings.quote: Removing existing statutory mitigations will have material financial consequences on revenue budgets and ultimately potentially impacting on capital investment programmes.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council planning to hold only £25.2 million in reserves to smooth a £75.5 million three-year budget gap—reserves are finite and will be depleted.
findings.detail: The updated Reserves Policy (December 2025) recommends holding an average of the three-year budget gap (£25.181 million) to smooth delivery of savings and provide one-off investment capacity. However, this provides less than four months of the annual budget gap at the envisaged rate. Once reserves are spent, the council has no buffer for pay overruns, funding shortfalls, or savings delivery delays.
findings.matters: Reserves are temporary. If savings are not delivered, reserves will be exhausted within 2–3 years, forcing the council into a position of being unable to set a balanced budget.
findings.figures: £25.181 million targeted balance, based on average of £75.545 million three-year gap
findings.quote: Therefore, as the envisaged three year gap equates to £75.545 million, an average of £25.181 million should be targeted.

findings.detail: The IJB approved its own MTFP in March 2026, showing budget gaps of £21.7–22.2m per year across 2027/28–2029/30. The council must fund this from its own budget. The document explicitly reminds members: 'elected members should continue to be mindful of the Council's contribution to the IJB in support of its cost and demand pressures when settling its budget for 2027/28 and beyond.'
findings.matters: Adult care is a demand-led, unfunded service. The council cannot choose to reduce IJB funding; this is a cost it must meet, narrowing its flexibility to manage its own budget gap.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Scottish Government funding assumed flat-cash, but 1% change equals £9.5 million budget impact; economic forecasters expect Local Government unlikely to be prioritised.
findings.detail: The council forecasts no real increase in core grant funding from Scottish Government, despite small cash increases announced in the Spending Review. The document notes explicitly: 'there is a risk of an actual reduction to previous cash settlements' depending on Scottish Government priorities. A 1% swing in funding creates a £9.5m budget impact, yet the forecast has no contingency for this.
findings.matters: If Scottish Government reduces funding (1% = £9.5m), the three-year budget gap widens by 12.6% or more, requiring emergency savings or accelerated reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: 1% funding change = £9.5 million impact, no assumption of additional resources above flat cash
findings.quote: Estimating future years' funding with any degree of certainty is challenging, and a slight variation on funding level can have a significant impact (1% equates to more than £9.500 million) on the Council's forecast financial position.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Pay award cost pressure of £20.6 million in 2027/28 alone, with range of £18.2 to £34.8 million depending on outcome of negotiations.
findings.detail: The council assumes 3% pay uplift for 2027/28–2028/29, reverting to 2% baseline thereafter. However, the pessimistic scenario assumes a 2.5% increase above envisaged, creating a £16.6m single-year swing. The council explicitly flags ongoing uncertainty due to economic effects of Middle East conflict. Pay is the largest single budget element; overruns cannot be absorbed elsewhere without service cuts.
findings.matters: Pay is the largest and most unpredictable cost. A pay award outcome worse than assumed would immediately worsen the budget gap by tens of millions, forcing emergency measures mid-year.
findings.figures: £20.600 million (envisaged 2027/28), £18.200 to £34.800 million (scenario range), £55.400 million (3-year envisaged)
findings.quote: a total of £20.600 million pay provision is estimated for 2027/28. Total provision over the next 3 years is anticipated to be £55.400 million.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32

Across scenario modelling, the gap ranges from £45.3m (optimistic) to £257.9m (pessimistic), demonstrating extreme sensitivity to pay and funding assumptions.
findings.matters: A gap of this magnitude cannot be closed through small efficiency savings. It requires material service reductions, significant Council Tax increases, or sustained reserve drawdown—all carrying credit and delivery risk.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Auditors found early retirement decisions for two senior officers lacked documented consideration of alternatives and value-for-money assessment
findings.detail: Two chief officers were granted early retirement in 2024/25 as part of restructuring that reduced chief officers from six to five. Auditors found that while alternatives were reportedly considered, this was documented as 'not applicable' with insufficient clarity on why alternatives were rejected or how value-for-money was assessed. Auditors recommended enhanced scrutiny and transparency, and the council plans a governance review by December 2026.
findings.matters: Lack of transparent decision documentation on senior exit costs raises questions about financial controls, governance rigour, and whether the council is achieving value-for-money in employment decisions.
findings.figures: Two chief officers early retirement; chief officer headcount reduced by one
findings.quote: auditors found that it was not always clear how the council had considered whether alternative options to early retirement would have: been feasible; and/or represented better value for money.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Council increased council tax by 10% in 2025/26, highest in recent years, to bridge modest budget gap
findings.detail: To address a 2025/26 General Fund budget gap of £13.6 million (1.2% of budget), the council raised council tax by 10%, significantly higher than the 5% increase in 2023/24 or 3% in 2022/23. This steep rise to solve a relatively small gap suggests limited headroom for future tax increases to close the larger gaps projected ahead.
findings.matters: Double-digit council tax increases signal taxpayer tolerance limits and constrain a council's primary revenue-raising tool; if 10% was necessary for a 1.2% gap, future larger gaps cannot be solved by tax alone.
findings.figures: 10% council tax increase for 2025/26 (£15.3m revenue); compares to 5% in 2023/24, 3% in 2022/23
findings.quote: The council increased council tax by ten per cent to bridge the budget gap for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Capital spend falling short of plans; council increases borrowing by £99 million while reprofiling delivery
findings.detail: Capital spending has been consistently lower than planned, driven by inflation and construction sector constraints. The council reprofiled £15.7 million from 2024/25 to later years of its five-year programme while increasing long-term borrowing from £590.6 million (March 2024) to £689.6 million (March 2025). The £856 million five-year capital investment programme is planned but delivery risk is evident.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Adult social care performance significantly weaker than other services; only 18% of indicators in top two quartiles
findings.detail: Performance across Local Government Benchmarking Framework indicators is mixed. Adult social work services performance is particularly weak, with only 18% of indicators in the top two quartiles versus 100% for housing and 50% for the council overall. The council has also seen sustained deterioration in satisfaction indicators since 2010/11, a 15-year downward trend that should concern any service user base assessment.
findings.matters: Weakening performance in demand-led services like adult social care often signals growing unmet need or service quality issues, both of which have budget implications and reputational risk; deteriorating satisfaction trends suggest eroding public confidence.
findings.figures: Adult social work: 18% of indicators in top two quartiles; satisfaction indicators declined since 2010/11 baseline
findings.quote: only 18 per cent of indicators for Adult social work services remain in the top two quartiles.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Reserves policy requires strategic review; council holds £282 million earmarked but strategy for use unclear
findings.detail: The council holds £346.3 million in total usable reserves, with £282.0 million earmarked for future budget pressures. The Accounts Commission specifically required the council to address auditor recommendations 'around reviewing its approach to the use of reserves' and 'to now set out clearly how it intends to close the budget gap'. The council has committed to a reserves review by June 2026. This signals auditor concern that reserves are being managed tactically rather than strategically.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on reserves to manage recurring budget gaps indicates the council is not living within sustainable revenue income; unclear strategy for reserve drawdown creates uncertainty about medium-term solvency.
findings.figures: £346.3m total usable reserves (2024/25); £282.0m earmarked General Fund balance
findings.quote: The council will need to ensure that it applies its reserves strategically. This will include reviewing how its reserves earmarked for future budget pressures can be used to support investment in long-term sustainability or improved outcomes.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Council's primary mitigation strategy—transformation—acknowledged to be insufficient to close budget gap alone
findings.detail: The council is investing £793.1 million through its Community Investment Fund (through 2033/34) and embedding transformation across all services. The Accounts Commission emphasises that benefits realisation is 'essential' given the 'increasing role that transformation needs to play in closing the budget gap'—signalling the Commission's concern that the council is relying on a strategy it knows is inadequate.
findings.matters: If the council cannot articulate how it will deliver the necessary savings beyond transformation, there is material execution risk to achieving financial sustainability and meeting loan covenants.
findings.figures: £793.1 million Community Investment Fund value through 2033/34
findings.quote: officers are clear that transformation will not close the budget gap alone.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £136.9 million over five years with no clear strategy articulated to close it
findings.detail: The council faces a General Fund cumulative budget gap of £136.9 million from 2026/27 to 2030/31 based on flat cash settlement, on top of the £20.6 million gap for 2025/26. The Controller of Audit explicitly states it is not yet clear how the council will address the widening gap. This becomes critical given the scale of the challenge and the inadequacy of current mitigation plans.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence that a council can achieve financial sustainability; a widening gap with no articulated solution is a red flag for service continuity and debt service risk.
findings.figures: £136.9m cumulative 2026/27–2030/31; £20.6m for 2025/26 (General Fund £13.6m + HRA £7.0m)
findings.quote: it is not yet clear how the council will fully address it. Given the scale of emerging challenges and the widening budget gap, a strategic shift is now essential to ensure continued financial sustainability and service delivery.
